paragraphs.text: Form No:HCJD/C-121 ORDER SHEET LAHORE HIGH COURT, Bahawalpur Bench, Bahawalpur JUDICIAL DEPARTMENT W. P. No.6712 of 2026 Habib Ullah Vs. Additional District Judge, etc. S.No. of order/ proceeding Date of order/ Proceeding. Order with signature of Judge, and that of parties or counsel, where necessary. 04.11.2026 Rao Nasir Mahmood Khan, Advocate for the petitioner. Through instant Constitutional Petition, the petitioner has called in question the order and memo of costs dated 14.04.2026 passed by the learned Rent Tribunal, whereby the ejectment petition instituted by respondent No.3 under the Punjab Rented Premises Act, 2009 (hereinafter referred to as the “Act”), was allowed, as well as the judgment and decree dated 13.10.2026 passed by the learned Appellate Court, whereby the appeal preferred by the petitioner was dismissed.

Brief facts of the case are that respondent No.3 instituted an ejectment petition against the petitioner and others under the Act, which was contested by tenants through submission of a written reply on various grounds. It is noteworthy that the respondent also made good the deficiency in compliance with the order passed by depositing the requisite fine in terms of Section 9-B of the Act. Initially, the ejectment petition was allowed vide order dated 24.09.2024; however, the said order was set aside by the learned Appellate Court with the direction to the learned Rent Tribunal to record the evidence of both parties and decide the matter afresh in accordance with law. Consequently, issues were framed and the evidence of the respondent was recorded. However, the petitioners failed to submit their affidavit in evidence in accordance with the procedure prescribed under the Act. Their subsequent application seeking permission to produce evidence was, therefore, dismissed by the learned Rent Tribunal. Upon conclusion of the proceedings, the learned Rent Tribunal allowed the ejectment petition vide order and memo of costs dated 14.04.2026, directing the tenants to vacate the rented premises within fifteen days and to pay rent at the rate of Rs.4,500/- per month with effect from October 2022 till vacation of the premises. The appeal preferred by the petitioner against the said order was dismissed by the learned Additional District Judge, Minchinabad, vide judgment and decree dated 13.10.2026. Hence, the instant petition.

Learned counsel for petitioner contends that impugned order and judgment and decree passed by the learned Courts below are contrary to law and facts, having been rendered without proper appreciation of the material available on record. It is argued that no relationship of landlord and tenant exists between the parties, as the petitioner and his brothers had themselves constructed the house in question and had been residing therein for a considerable period. The registered Waqf Deed dated 25.04.2019 and the subsequent Mutation No.1053 have also been challenged through a separate civil suit, whereas the rent agreements relied upon by respondent No.3 are alleged to be fabricated documents. Learned counsel further contends that the learned Courts below failed to appreciate the jurisdictional bar contained in Section 2(a) of the Act, as the subject property admittedly forms part of a Waqf estate and is being utilized for religious purposes. The competency and locus standi of respondent No.3 to institute the ejectment proceedings have also been questioned. It is maintained that the learned Courts below passed the impugned orders in a hasty manner, without examining the material legal and factual objections raised by the petitioner, thereby occasioning a miscarriage of justice. Hence, the impugned orders are liable to be set aside.
Arguments heard. Record perused with the able assistance of learned counsel for the petitioner.

The controversy, in the first instance, requires determination of objection regarding the applicability of the Act to the property in question. The principal contention of learned counsel for the petitioner is that since the demised property forms part of a Waqf estate and is connected with a Mosque or Madrasah, the same falls within the exclusion contemplated under Section 2(a) of the Act and, consequently, the learned Rent Tribunal lacked jurisdiction to entertain the ejectment petition. The contention, however, does not appear to be legally sustainable.

A plain reading of Section 2(a) of the Act indicates that the exclusion relating to a place of religious worship is confined to premises which, by their nature and use, constitute a place where religious worship is actually performed. The mere fact that the ownership of a property vests in a Waqf estate or that its rental income is intended to be utilized for religious or charitable purposes does not, by itself, transform every portion of such estate into a place of religious worship. The distinction between the principal place of worship and its independent ancillary or commercial premises cannot be overlooked. The applicability of rent legislation is to be determined with reference to the nature and character of the demised premises and the purpose for which the same have been let out, rather than merely the status of their ownership. In the present case, the premises in question comprise a commercial shop/room, which was allegedly let out for commercial and residential use, and there is nothing on record to establish that the demised portion itself is being utilized as a Mosque, prayer hall or any other place where religious rites are performed. Accordingly, the mere circumstance that the property forms part of a Waqf estate cannot bring it within the exclusion contemplated under Section 2(a) of the Act. The demised premises, therefore, fall within the statutory concept of a building under Section 2(a) and premises under Section 2(f) of the Act. Reliance can be placed upon case titled as “WAHEED YOUNAS Vs. ADDITIONAL DISTRICT JUDGE, GUJRANWALA and 3 others” (PLD 2024 Lahore 608).

The above conclusion is further fortified by Section 3 of the Act, which contemplates exemption of premises from the operation of the Act through a notification issued by the Provincial Government in the official Gazette. No such notification specifically exempting the subject premises from the operation of the Act has been brought on record. In the absence of such notification, the petitioner cannot claim exemption merely on the basis of the Waqf character of the property. Thus, the objection regarding the lack of jurisdiction of the learned Rent Tribunal is devoid of force.

The objection concerning the competency and locus standi of respondent No.3 also merits consideration. Under Section 2(d) of the Act, a landlord includes a person who is for the time being entitled or authorized to receive rent in respect of the premises. The definition is not confined exclusively to the owner of the property; rather, it also encompasses a person lawfully authorized to administer the premises and receive rent on behalf of the person or institution entitled thereto. In circumstances of the present case, respondent No.3 claims his authority on the basis of the registered Waqf Deed dated 25.04.2019, whereby the administration of the subject property was entrusted to him as Mutawalli. A Mutawalli, being responsible for management and administration of Waqf property, may lawfully institute proceedings for protection and recovery of such property, provided that requisite authority is established. Reliance can be placed upon the case-laws titled as “Messrs PHIPSONS COMPANY (PVT.) LIMITED through Adnan Maqbool Khan Vs. ZAHID MOYEEN and 2 others” (PLD 2026 Lahore 172) and “SHAHZAD Vs. REHAN DAR and others” (2026 CLC 1150). The administration of Waqf property and utilization of its income for the purposes of the endowment are recognized under the Punjab Waqf Properties Ordinance, 1979. The principle underlying the management and preservation of Waqf property has also been considered by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in case titled as “SIKANDAR HAYAT KHAN JOGAZAI and others Vs. MUHAMMAD HASHIM and others” (PLD 2019 SC 730). Consequently, where the Mutawalli is duly authorized to administer the property and receive rent, his competency to invoke the statutory remedy cannot be defeated merely because he is not the personal owner of the demised premises. In the present case, the registered Waqf Deed, coupled with the evidence produced by respondent No.3, sufficiently supports his asserted authority for purposes of the proceedings before the learned Rent Tribunal.

Another objection raised by learned counsel for the petitioner relates to the denial of the relationship of landlord and tenant by claiming that he is residing at rented premises as owner. It is noteworthy that the stance adopted by the petitioner is self-contradictory. On the one hand, he has categorically denied the relationship of landlord and tenant by asserting that the property was constructed by him and his brothers and that they are its owners; on the other hand, he seeks to invoke the exclusion contemplated under Section 2(a) of the Act on the ground that the demised premises form part of a Waqf estate and are being utilized for religious purposes. These two pleas, when examined in the context of the controversy, do not appear to be mutually reconcilable. If petitioner claims independent ownership and denies the very existence of tenancy, he cannot, without establishing the factual and legal basis thereof, simultaneously seek protection against the operation of rent legislation by relying upon the alleged religious character of the premises. Such inconsistent pleas, particularly in the absence of any supporting evidence, considerably weaken the credibility of his defence. Needless to observe that the petitioner was required to substantiate his respective objections through cogent evidence, rather than merely raising mutually inconsistent assertions to defeat the ejectment proceedings.

Attending the other aspects of controversy, it transpires from the record that although the petitioner categorically denied the relationship of landlord and tenant, he failed to substantiate his stance through legally admissible evidence. It is an admitted position that, after the matter was remanded by the learned Appellate Court, the learned Rent Tribunal afforded the parties an opportunity to lead evidence. The respondent duly availed the said opportunity, whereas the petitioner failed to submit his affidavit in evidence in accordance with the procedure prescribed under the Act. His subsequent application seeking permission to produce evidence was also dismissed by the learned Rent Tribunal. No material has been brought before this Court to demonstrate that the said order was passed in violation of any mandatory provision of law or that the petitioner was unlawfully deprived of an opportunity to substantiate his defence. A party who, despite being afforded an opportunity, fails to lead evidence cannot subsequently seek to discredit the proceedings merely on the ground that its own version was not accepted. The learned Rent Tribunal was, therefore, justified in deciding the controversy on the basis of the evidence actually available on record.

On the other hand, respondent No.3 himself appeared as AW-1 and supported the averments made in the ejectment petition. He also produced AW-2 and AW-3 in corroboration of his stance. The registered Waqf Deed dated 25.04.2019 was relied upon to establish his status and authority as Mutawalli, whereas the rent agreements, exhibited as Ex.A2, Ex.A3 and Ex.A4, were produced to substantiate the relationship of landlord and tenant between the parties. The fact that the said agreements were registered with the relevant Police Station was also brought on record. The respondent further established the default committed by the tenants in payment of rent, which constituted an independent ground for seeking their ejectment under the relevant provisions of the Act. The aforesaid evidence, when examined collectively, lends support to the respondent’s case. The petitioner, despite denying the execution and authenticity of rent agreements, did not produce any affirmative evidence to establish that the documents were fabricated or that the parties were otherwise related in a manner inconsistent with the asserted tenancy. Mere institution of a separate civil suit challenging the Waqf Deed and Mutation No.1053 does not, by itself, render the said documents ineffective or suspend the proceedings before Rent Tribunal, particularly when no order of a competent Court restraining such proceedings or otherwise affecting operation of relevant documents has been brought to the notice of this Court. Needless to observe that the Rent Tribunal was required to examine relationship of landlord and tenant and the grounds of ejectment on the basis of the material available before it, and not to adjudicate upon the ultimate title to the Waqf property.

The learned Rent Tribunal correctly accepted the petition while keeping in view the relevant material as well as law and the learned Appellate Court has also examined controversy and found no justification to interfere with the findings recorded by the learned Rent Tribunal. The petitioner has not been able to identify any misreading or non- reading of material evidence, misapplication of relevant statutory provisions or jurisdictional defect in the concurrent findings of the learned Courts below. It is settled that constitutional jurisdiction is not intended to provide another forum for reappraisal of evidence or substitution of one possible view for another, particularly where findings recorded by the forums below are supported by the material available on record and suffer from no patent illegality or jurisdictional infirmity.

In view of the foregoing discussion, this Court is of the considered opinion that the objection regarding the applicability of the Act to the subject premises is misconceived; respondent No.3 has sufficiently established his authority to institute ejectment proceedings; and the petitioner, having failed to substantiate his defence through evidence despite being afforded an opportunity, cannot derive any benefit from his own omission. The impugned order and memo of costs dated 14.04.2026, as well as the judgment and decree dated 13.10.2026, do not suffer from any illegality, material irregularity, misreading or non-reading of evidence warranting interference by this Court in its constitutional jurisdiction.
For the reasons recorded above, finding no merit in the instant Constitutional Petition, the same is hereby dismissed in limine. (Syed Ahsan Raza Kazmi) Judge Approved for reporting. Judge Ejaz*
